'''Grigor Gurzadyan''' ({{langx|hy|Գրիգոր Գուրզադյան}}) (15 October 1922 – 22 February 2014)  was an [[Armenians|Armenian]] astronomer, and pioneer of space astronomy.

== Life ==
Gurzadyan was born in 1922 in Baghdad, to parents that survived the [[Armenian genocide]]. Upon graduating from the Hydrotechnical and Constructional Department of [[State Engineering University of Armenia|Yerevan Polytechnic Institute]] in 1944, he became a graduate student of [[Victor Ambartsumian]], who had just moved to Armenia. Being in Ambartsumian’s founding team of [[Byurakan Observatory]], he later headed a Laboratory, in 1960s became deputy director of the Observatory for space research. Then, he headed the branch of Byurakan observatory on space research. In 1971 he founded and headed the [[Garni Space Astronomy Laboratory]] (Institute, 1992–2004). 
Member of [[Armenian National Academy of Sciences]] (1986; corresponding member 1965), DSci. 1955, PhD 1948.
His son is [[Vahe Gurzadyan]], mathematical physicist and a professor at Yerevan Physics Institute, whose main research topics are: the chaos in non-linear systems, N-body dynamics, stellar dynamics, Cosmic Microwave Background radiation, observational cosmology.

== Works ==
[[File:Գրիգոր Գուրզադյանի կիսանդրին ԵՊՀ-ում.jpg|thumb|Gurzadyan's bust at Yerevan State University]]
In 1960s and early 1970s he directed the UV and X-ray observations of the Sun via [[Rocket Astrophysical Observatories K-2, K-3 and K-4]] by means of [[ballistic rockets R-5]]; the first launch being on 15 February 1961 from [[Kapustin Yar]] military base in Russia.  His paper in ''Comm. Armenian Acad. Sciences'', XLIII, 28, 1966, “''A Powerful X-ray Flare on the Sun''” (of 1 October 1965) is on the detection of most powerful Solar X-ray flare observed by then.

Then he moved to design space orbital observatories, both on board automatic probes and crewed spacecraft. Ultraviolet telescope ''Procyon'' was on board [[Kosmos (satellite)|Kosmos]] 309 in 1969, and X-ray telescope ''Altair'' on board [[Meteor (satellite)|Meteor]] 1–16 in 1974; both were launched from [[Plesetsk cosmodrome]]. [[Orion 1 Space Observatory]] (see [[Orion 1 and Orion 2 Space Observatories]])  the first space telescope with an objective prism, was installed in April 1971 onboard the first space station [[Salyut 1]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Gurzadyan | first1 = G.A | last2 = Ohanesyan | first2 = J.B. | year = 1972 | title = Observed Energy Distribution of alpha Lyra and beta Cen at 2000–3800 Å | journal = Nature | volume = 239 | issue = 5367| page = 90 | doi=10.1038/239090a0|bibcode = 1972Natur.239...90G | doi-access = free }}</ref> The highlight was [[Orion 2 Space Observatory]] (see [[Orion 1 and Orion 2 Space Observatories]]),  with a wide-angle meniscus telescope of the Cassegrain system, operated on board the spacecraft [[Soyuz 13]] in December 1973.  Spectra of thousands of stars to as faint as 13th magnitude were obtained,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Gurzadyan | first1 = G.A. | year = 1974 | title = Ultraviolet spectra of Capella | journal = Nature | volume = 250 | issue = 5463| pages = 204–205 | doi=10.1038/250204a0|bibcode = 1974Natur.250..204G | s2cid = 4225026 }}</ref> the first satellite UV spectrogram of a [[planetary nebula]] ([[IC 2149]]) was obtained, revealing lines of aluminum  and  titanium - elements not previously observed in [[planetary nebulae]], [[two photon emission]] from nebulae was detected for the first time.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Gurzadyan | first1 = G.A. | year = 1976 | title = Two-photon emission in planetary nebula IC 2149 | journal = Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific | volume = 88 | page = 891 | doi=10.1086/130041 | bibcode= }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Gurzadyan | first1 = G.A. | last2 = Rustambekova | first2 = S.S. | year = 1975 | title = Silicon-rich stellar envelope? | journal = Nature | volume = 254 | issue = 5498| pages = 311–312 | doi=10.1038/254311a0|bibcode = 1975Natur.254..311G | s2cid = 4197408 }}</ref>
For comparison, the [[Skylab]]’s UV telescope which was on the orbit at the same time, could only look at stars down to 7.5th magnitude.  

He predicted magnetic fields in [[planetary nebulae]] in 1960s, which were actually discovered in 2005 (Jordan, Werner, O’Toole). He authored theoretical papers on [[flare stars]] (predicted negative infrared flares), interstellar matter, binary stars. In 1990s he developed the theory of common chromospheres (''roundchromes'') of close binary stars and of evolution of binary globular clusters.

For decades he lectured in [[Yerevan State University]] (theoretical astrophysics, celestial mechanics) and in Yerevan Polytechnic Institute (precise mechanics). He is also known as an original painter and for his essays on [[philosophy of science]] and art.

Gurzadyan died on 22 February 2014 in [[Yerevan]]. His requiem service was attended by the President of [[Armenia]] and the service was held by Supreme Patriarch and Catholicos of all Armenians.<ref name="AN">{{cite web|url=http://armenianow.com/news/52238/armenia_astrophysicist_grigor_gurzadyan_dies|title=Prominent Armenian astrophysicist Grigor Gurzadyan dies at 91|date=2014-02-24|publisher=[[ArmeniaNow]]|access-date=24 February 2014|archive-date=2014-03-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140301105709/http://armenianow.com/news/52238/armenia_astrophysicist_grigor_gurzadyan_dies|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="AP">{{cite news|url=http://armenpress.am/eng/news/751363/|title=Armenia's President attends requiem of Grigor Gurzadyan|date=February 24, 2014|publisher=[[Armenpress]]|access-date=24 February 2014}}</ref>
